blocks.content: Linux namespaces are the kernel feature that gives a container its own isolated view of the system, its own processes, its own network, its own filesystem mounts, while every container on a host actually shares one underlying kernel.
1. Six Namespace Types, Each Isolating One Resource
blocks.text: 1. Six Namespace Types, Each Isolating One Resource

blocks.content: A container is not isolated by one single mechanism, it is the combination of six different namespace types, each responsible for hiding one specific kind of system resource from view: PID (processes), network, mount (filesystem), UTS (hostname), IPC (inter-process communication), and user (user/group IDs).

blocks.alt: Six distinct namespace types, each covering one resource

blocks.content: Inside its own PID namespace, a container's main process typically sees itself as PID 1, the very first process in its own isolated process tree, entirely unaware of any other processes running on the host. From the host's perspective, that same process has an entirely ordinary, much larger PID.

blocks.alt: The same process, two entirely different PIDs depending on perspective

blocks.content:
# Inside the container
ps aux
# PID 1 is the container's own main process

# On the host
ps aux | grep <process name>
# The same process shows up with a normal host PID, not 1

code.content:
# Inside the container
ps aux
# PID 1 is the container's own main process

# On the host
ps aux | grep <process name>
# The same process shows up with a normal host PID, not 1

codes.bash:

blocks.content: A network namespace gives a container its own network interfaces, its own IP address, and its own routing table, entirely separate from the host's, exactly what makes the container networking covered in the Docker Networking module possible in the first place.

blocks.alt: A private network stack, entirely its own

blocks.content: A mount namespace gives a container its own view of what is mounted where, this is the foundational mechanism underneath the union filesystem covered later in this module, without it, a container could not have its own independent filesystem view at all.

blocks.alt: An independent view of the filesystem, mount by mount

blocks.content: None of these namespaces individually is "a container," a container is really just a regular Linux process, started inside a specific combination of all six namespace types at once, which is what gives it the complete illusion of running on its own isolated machine.

blocks.alt: Combined together, they are what a container actually is

blocks.content: Under the hood, namespaces are created via the clone() system call (with specific flags for each namespace type) or the standalone unshare command, this is the exact low-level mechanism runc, covered later in this module, uses when it actually starts a container's process.

blocks.alt: The actual system call that creates a namespace

blocks.title: Key Takeaway
points: Six namespace types (PID, network, mount, UTS, IPC, user) each isolate one specific system resource, combined together they are what makes a process a container.
A container's main process typically sees itself as PID 1 inside its own PID namespace, while the host sees it as an entirely ordinary process.
